ES.2 Background, Purpose, and Objectives Water and wastewater treatment facilities consume 3% of all energy in the U.S., but reductions in electricity consumption, chemical input, greenhouse gas emissions, as well as improved energy recovery, and smaller design safety factors for more precise designs could be realized with improvements in process monitoring and control. Current water resource recovery facility (WRRF) data collection, monitoring, and control approaches use 20th century process monitoring and control systems, which require large design safety factors to ensure reliability in the absence of more advanced, precise controls. Implementation of modern data-driven control tools (sensors, algorithms, decision support methods) can lead to more efficient operations that provide intrinsic reliability with better overall process performance at full-scale (increased resource recovery, higher quality effluent). The purpose of this report is to highlight a project in which five emerging WRRF process technologies (referred to as “Applications” throughout this report) with the potential to maximize energy recovery from wastewater and minimize both electrical and intrinsic energy demand served as testbeds to develop methods and demonstrate the impact of this digital design revolution. Integration of Data Driven Process Control for Maximizing Energy and Resource Efficiency in WRRFs xvii The objectives of this project are to: 1. Develop and demonstrate data-driven process controls in real full-scale facilities for five promising Applications that provide a whole plant approach and offer substantial energy and resource recovery benefits. 2. Create an ML Toolkit of new process control approaches along with an implementation guide of five examples for application at utilities across the U.S. As shown in Figure ES-1, the five promising WRRF Applications and their host utilities are: 1. Carbon diversion: high-rate contact stabilization (DC Water) 2. Biological nutrient removal (BNR): ammonia-based aeration control (ABAC) / ammonia vs. NOx (AvN) + partial denitrification with anammox (PdNA) (HRSD) 3. Disinfection: peracetic acid (PAA) (Metro Water Recovery) 4. P-recovery: MagPrex® (Metro Water Recovery) 5. Holistic biosolids optimization (DC Water) This project advances the above objectives through the following seven tasks which are part of the Statement of Project Objectives (SOPO): • Task 1: Experimental Design and Data Collection (Chapters 5.x.3 Get Data) • Task 2: Data and Process Analysis (Chapters 5.x.4 Prepare Data) • Task 3: Modeling and Machine Learning (Chapters 5.x.5 Train Model) • Task 4: Pilot-scale Implementation (Chapters 5.x.6 Deploy Model) • Task 5: TEA and LCA (Chapter 6, Appendix A) • Task 6: Data-driven Process Controls Toolbox (Chapter 1.4 ML Toolkit) • Task 7: Outreach and Technology Transfer (Appendix B) Tasks 1-5 address Objective 1, and Tasks 6-7 address Objective 2. The report chapters that cover each of the seven tasks are noted in parentheses above. A final task and milestone table for the project is provided in Appendix C. The implementation of data-driven process controls for these five technologies supports DOE EERE’s and IEDO’s mission to accelerate the innovation and adoption of cost-effective technologies that eliminate industrial greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.
